prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: Code · Config options with long tokens (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Option" · longest unbreakable word 131px · one-line width 131px
  col 2: header "Default" · longest unbreakable word 90px · one-line width 334px
  col 3: header "Example" · longest unbreakable word 537px · one-line width 537px
  col 4: header "Description" · longest unbreakable word 83px · one-line width 501px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 720px. You MAY choose a total wider than 719px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"good","why":"Sensible pecking order: Option keeps its 131px identifier intact, Default is trimmed to what it needs, and the leftover space goes to Description, which reads in 2–3 clean lines. Rows stay compact and comparable. The cost is the Example column (~190px), where the postgres URL and JWKS URL break into 3 lines, though at tolerable points (after dots/slashes) rather than mid-word fragments."},"B":{"grade":"poor","why":"Example is given ~300px while Description is squeezed to roughly 110px, so prose collapses into 4–5 short lines and the table becomes very tall and ragged on the right. The URL still breaks inside a word (\"internal.e / xample.com\"), so the width spent on Example buys little."},"C":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Example at ~300px gets the URLs down to two lines and Description is a bit wider than B, so the right side is less shredded. But Description is still narrow enough to run 3–4 lines, and the URL break leaves a line starting with \".example.com:5432/production_main\", which reads awkwardly and is easy to misread when copying."},"D":{"grade":"poor","why":"Space is wasted on Default (~150px for content whose longest token is 90px) while Description is crushed to ~110px and runs to five lines per row.
